spec.description: Create an EventSub subscription: the event type to listen for, the condition saying whose events those are, and the transport to deliver them over. For the WebSocket transport that transport names the `session_id` from the `session_welcome` message of an open socket, and the events then arrive on that socket. Answered `202 Accepted` with the subscription as created.

request.title: CreateSubscriptionRequest
request.description: The subscription to create. Sent as a JSON body.

type.description: The subscription type to create, such as `stream.online`, `channel.follow` or `channel.chat.message`.

version.description: The version of that subscription type, such as `1` or `2`. Which versions exist is a fact about the type.

condition.description: The parameter values for this subscription type: `broadcaster_user_id`, `user_id`, `moderator_user_id` and so on. Which keys are required, and which scopes they need, is a fact about the subscription type.

additionalProperties.description: One condition value, always a string on the wire.

transport.title: CreateSubscriptionTransport
transport.description: Where Twitch should deliver this subscription's notifications.

method.description: The transport method. `websocket` is the one this client opens a socket for.

session_id.description: The WebSocket session to deliver to, for `websocket`: the `id` of the `session_welcome` message that opened the socket.

callback.description: The HTTPS callback URL to deliver to, for `webhook`. Port 443, no redirects.

secret.description: The secret Twitch signs webhook deliveries with, for `webhook`: 10 to 100 ASCII characters. Never recorded; see the notes.

conduit_id.description: The conduit to deliver to, for `conduit`.

response.title: CreateSubscriptionFrame
response.description: The wire frame: the one subscription just created, and what the application has spent on subscriptions in total.

data.description: A list holding the one subscription created.

total.description: How many subscriptions the application currently has.

total_cost.description: The sum of every subscription's cost.

max_total_cost.description: The most the application is allowed to spend on subscriptions.

unverified.detail: No recording yet: Helix authenticates every call, and the machine this spec was written on holds no Twitch application credentials. The Record workflow fills this in: it reads the application client id and secret from the repository secrets TWITCH_CLIENT_ID and TWITCH_CLIENT_SECRET, mints an app access token through the core, replays this endpoint's `examples/*.request.json` with `truewire capture`, and opens a pull request with the response the API sent.

notes: The response schema is the wire frame and no `envelope.payload` is declared, so the method returns the frame: `total`, `total_cost` and `max_total_cost` sit beside `data` and are answers a caller wants, not an envelope to index past (authoring rule 6).

This is the one endpoint here that needs a *user* access token, which is what `meta: {"token": "user"}` declares: the reference is explicit that a WebSocket subscription created with an app access token fails, and the client credentials flow cannot mint a user token. The core refuses the call before making a request when the client holds none. That also means the Record workflow, which mints an app access token, cannot record this endpoint; the `unverified` block stands until somebody records it with a user token.

`transport.secret` is a credential and belongs to the `webhook` transport, which this client does not use. It is declared because the request body has it, and a recorded example must never carry a real one.

`status` on a subscription is left a bare string rather than an `enum`. The reference lists the values twice, in the filter parameter and in the response body, and the two lists differ: `websocket_failed_to_reconnect` and `conduit_deleted` appear in one and not the other. A guessed `Literal` would reject a status Twitch already sends, so the filter parameter — where an invalid value is a `400` and a `Literal` genuinely helps — declares the enum and the response field does not. `truewire check` warns about the response field on every run; the warning is correct that this may be a closed set, and wrong that the closed set is known.

Written from the Helix reference at the `docs` URL above. Fields the reference marks deprecated are not declared; an undeclared field passes validation and is dropped from the validated value, so a recording that carries one is still valid. The first recording confirms or corrects the rest.
